Hi Tim —

Thanks again for the conversation earlier this week. As promised, attaching a draft SLA template and a simple credit/escrow example so we can walk through numbers. High-level proposal below so your procurement/legal teams can triage quickly: 

- Baseline uptime (standard): 99.9% monthly
- Optional premium tier for critical workloads: 99.95% (requires minimum monthly commitment / higher rate)
- Monthly service credits: slab-based model (see attached spreadsheet) with a per-month cap set as a percentage of monthly invoice
- Credit escrow: option to establish an escrow pool (prefunded) to apply credits automatically without separate credit memos
- Maintenance carveouts: scheduled maintenance windows excluded; emergency maintenance handled under defined notification windows

Please review SLA_Template_v1.2.pdf and the accompanying credit-escrow-example.xlsx and let me know what items you want to change. If you prefer, we can include a clause for a pilot period at 99.95 for a single environment.

Ben —

Thanks for the quick turnaround and the attachments. A couple of clarifying questions from procurement/legal: 

1) Can you show a worked example of monthly credits for a ~$120k/month invoice under both 99.9% and 99.95%? We want to understand customer economics (not just percentages).
2) How would the escrow pool be funded and reconciled? Is it refundable? What happens to unused escrow funds?
3) We typically insist on a monthly cap equal to 50% of the monthly invoice for SaaS credits. Is that something Redwood can accept, or would you propose a different cap for premium tiers?

Also, legal flagged the maintenance carveout language as a bit broad — they asked that scheduled maintenance require 72 hours notice and emergency maintenance be limited to explicit security/operational fixes with post-event reporting.

If you can reply with a marked-up template and the worked example, I can circulate to the rest of the team.

Thanks, Tim — good questions. Quick responses and a proposed path forward below. Also see the attached examples Ben shared.

Worked-example (summary):
- For $120,000/mo invoice (example):
  - 99.9% uptime: allowable downtime ~43.2 minutes/month. If downtime exceeds that, credits calculated on the slab in credit-escrow-example.xlsx. Under the slab model, a single incident that drops monthly uptime to between 99.5%–99.9% would generate X% credit (see spreadsheet). Rough ballpark: credits in that band produce ~10–30% of monthly invoice depending on severity.
  - 99.95% uptime: allowable downtime ~21.6 minutes/month. Credits trigger at narrower bands; we expect smaller credit percentages but note this tier requires a written monthly minimum commit or a price uplift.

Escrow mechanics (proposal):
- Option A (prefund): CobaltSystems funds an escrow pool equal to 1x monthly average spend at contract signature. Credits are applied directly against that pool; Redwood reconciles monthly and replenishment is triggered when pool dips below 25% of target. Unused funds at contract termination are returned after final reconciliation.
- Option B (invoiced credit memos): No prefund. Redwood issues credit memos and applies them to future invoices; monthly credit cap still applies.

Cap policy: We are open to a 50% monthly cap as a starting point for the standard tier if CobaltSystems is comfortable with the slab percentages. For the 99.95 premium tier we typically propose a lower monthly cap (25% of monthly invoice) because the uplifted price reduces the frequency/severity of credits.

Maintenance carveouts: We can tighten the language to require 72-hour notice for scheduled maintenance and define emergency maintenance narrowly (security P0, urgent infra fixes). We'll add mandatory post-event RCA within 5 business days for emergency events.

Next steps I propose:
- Ben to share a marked-up SLA with the 50% cap language and a 99.95 optional schedule appended.
- Redwood legal and finance will draft the escrow flow (Option A) and provide a short appendix for procurement.

If that sounds acceptable, Ben/Laura and I will produce a redline and a short cover note for your legal.

Best,

Priya / Ben —

Quick internal note before we send the redline back: I prefer we move the credit schedule from a continuous linear model to discrete slabs (it reduces disputes and is easier for procurement to audit). Example slabs: >99.95 (no credit), 99.9–99.95 (10% credit), 99.5–99.9 (25% credit), <99.5 (50% credit). That maps nicely to a 50% monthly cap for the standard tier and 25% cap for the premium tier.

Also suggest we ask Finance to sign off on prefund escrow flow — we need clarity on cash handling and refunds. I'll loop in finance if you both agree.

--Laura
